There is very little data for any of the component properties of thermal diffusivity in the high temperature gamma phase region, which means that this attempt is tenuous at best. Therefore, it is stressed that although the authors have attempted to use data where possible, ultimately only model behavioral trends are expressed to facilitate discussion and not to be taken as definitive. The thermal conductivity (driven by the electrical component) of uranium has been shown to decrease quickly with increased Mo content in the first several wt.%Mo and decrease more slowly toward the center of the phase diagram (Nordheim 1931a, 1931b). Another way of saying this is that the thermal conductivity of a single phase would tend to be curved with with a minimum at the ∼50:50 atomic percent ratio and end members at the pure phase quantities. These decreases would be mitigated by the slowly and linearly decreasing density and the increasing specific heat capacity. The exact trends of these quantities are not individually known given a derth of verifying data, but these trends are shown notionally to assist in visualizing the broad changes. For instance, the final guiding-line shown in Figure 7 for both thermal conductivity and diffusivity does attempt to be somewhat physical, following acceptable functional forms. Though simplified in construction and true depth, the trend is consistent with the limited data, the functionality of the Nordheim (1931) relation for simple solid solutions, and its correspondence with thermal conductivity in metals.
